stem: A pregnant 28-year-old's husband has a fully penetrant autosomal dominant disease. On the family's marker gel, the husband and his affected father each show bands 1 and 2, while the husband's unaffected mother and unaffected sister each show band 1 only. The marker lies 10 map units from the disease gene. Chorionic villus sampling shows the fetus has bands 1 and 2, and the wife has band 1 only.
oneliner: 28F pregnant + husband with fully penetrant AD disease + gel: affected men 1,2, unaffected women 1 only + marker 10% recombination + fetus 1,2 → fetal risk?
ask: What is the risk that the fetus has the disease?

whyNot.A: Corresponds to **1% recombination**; this marker has **10%**
whyNot.C: The chance of **recombination**, which would apply to a fetus with band 1 and not band 2
whyNot.D: The **prior risk** before the marker; the fetus has the band that travels with disease
whyNot.E: Would require **1% recombination**; with 10% the marker is less tight

why: On the gel the **affected** relatives have band 2 and the **unaffected** relatives only band 1, so **band 2 travels with the disease allele**. The fetus has band 2 (from the father, since the wife has band 1 only). Risk = 1 - recombination fraction = 1 - 0.10 = **90%**.

idea.rule: The marker allele that travels with disease gives risk 1 minus the recombination fraction.
also: The fetus with band 1 only would have a 10% risk

stem: A 30-year-old tall man seeks help for infertility. He has small, firm, painless testes and mild gynecomastia, with azoospermia and high FSH and LH. A testicular biopsy is taken.
oneliner: 30M + tall + infertile + small firm testes + gynecomastia + azoospermia + high FSH and LH → what does the biopsy show?
ask: Which finding is expected on testicular biopsy?

options.E: Leydig cell tumor with Reinke crystals

whyNot.A: Gives azoospermia but **normal-sized testes** and normal FSH or only slightly raised levels
whyNot.B: A **painless testicular mass**, not small firm testes
whyNot.D: Gives a **painful, inflamed testis**; his testes are painless and small
whyNot.E: Gives a **testicular mass** with excess androgen or estrogen, not shrunken firm testes

answer: Sclerosed, hyalinized seminiferous tubules with clusters of Leydig cells (Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY)
why: In **Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)** the seminiferous tubules **hyalinize and sclerose** and there is **azoospermia** with raised FSH and LH. Leydig cells appear **clustered** but make less testosterone.

idea.rule: Klinefelter testis: sclerosed tubules, Leydig clumps, high FSH and LH.
also: Higher risk of male breast cancer

stem: An electron micrograph of a nucleus shows dark, densely packed clumps along the periphery and pale, loosely packed chromatin in the center. The dark regions carry deacetylated histones and methylated DNA, and the inactive X chromosome appears in this form.
oneliner: EM nucleus + dark peripheral clumps + deacetylated histones + methylated DNA + inactive X → what are the clumps?
ask: What are the dark peripheral clumps?

whyNot.B: The **pale, loosely packed** region that is transcriptionally active
whyNot.C: A round dark body, the site of **rRNA synthesis**; it is highly active
whyNot.D: A **thin protein layer** lining the envelope; it holds no DNA, so it cannot carry methylated DNA
whyNot.E: **Newly made pre-mRNA** at the edge of chromatin, a sign of active transcription

why: **Heterochromatin** is **densely packed**, dark on EM and **transcriptionally inactive**, with **histone deacetylation and DNA methylation**; the Barr body is an example. **Euchromatin** is open and active.

idea.rule: Dark and dense means silent; pale and open means active.
also: DNA methylation at CpG islands silences genes

stem: A 28-year-old man has chronic sinusitis and infertility with immotile sperm. An electron micrograph cross-section of a projection from his airway epithelial cells shows nine outer microtubule doublets around two central single microtubules, but the dynein arms on the outer doublets are missing.
oneliner: 28M + chronic sinusitis + infertile + immotile sperm + EM: nine doublets, central pair, no dynein arms → which structure?
ask: Which structure does this cross-section show?

whyNot.E: Nine doublets but **no central pair** (9+0), non-motile, sensory

answer: Motile cilium (9+2 axoneme), here lacking dynein arms
why: A motile cilium has a **9+2 axoneme**, nine outer doublets around a central pair, and **dynein arms** drive bending. Their loss causes **primary ciliary dyskinesia** (Kartagener syndrome) with sinusitis and infertility.

also: Kartagener syndrome: situs inversus, sinusitis, bronchiectasis
Dynein moves toward the minus end of microtubules
Kinesin moves toward the plus end
Sperm flagellum has the same 9+2 core

stem: A 12-year-old boy has an inherited condition. In the family pedigree, drawn with squares for males and circles for females, shaded symbols appear in three consecutive generations. His father and grandfather are also affected, severity differs between them, and roughly half of each affected person's children are affected. Unaffected relatives have only unaffected children, and an affected father has an affected son.
oneliner: 12M + shaded symbols in 3 generations + father-to-son transmission + about half of children affected + varying severity → which pattern?
ask: Which inheritance pattern does the pedigree show?

whyNot.B: An affected father passes it to **all daughters and no sons**, so father-to-son transmission excludes it
whyNot.C: Usually **skips generations** and needs two carrier parents; affected people are mostly in one generation
whyNot.D: Passes only from **mothers**, to all children, never from an affected father
whyNot.E: Mostly affects males via **carrier mothers**, no male-to-male transmission

why: **Every generation** is affected, **male-to-male transmission** occurs, and about **half** of the children are affected, which fits **autosomal dominant** inheritance. Different severity among relatives is **variable expressivity**.

idea.rule: Every generation, male-to-male transmission and half the children affected: autosomal dominant.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has MCAD deficiency, an autosomal recessive disease. An 87 base pair PCR product spanning the mutation is cut by NcoI into 61 and 26 base pair pieces only when the mutation is present. On the gel, the boy shows only the 61 and 26 bp bands and both parents show 87, 61 and 26 bp bands. His healthy sister's lane shows a single 87 bp band.
oneliner: 4M with MCAD deficiency; mutant allele cut 87 → 61 + 26 bp; he has cut bands only, parents all three; healthy sister one 87 bp band → her genotype?
ask: Which genotype does the sister's lane represent?

whyNot.A: Matches the **boy's lane**: only the 61 and 26 bp pieces
whyNot.B: Would show **87 plus 61 and 26 bp**, like each parent
whyNot.C: Would show **only cut bands**, like the boy, not a single 87 bp band
whyNot.E: Would be **affected** and carry the cut allele; she is healthy with no cut bands

why: The mutation **creates a restriction site**, so the mutant allele is **cut** and the normal allele stays **87 bp**. A single 87 bp band means **no mutant allele**, so she is homozygous normal; both parents are carriers.

idea.rule: A restriction site gained by mutation: cut = mutant, uncut = normal.
also: Carrier: both uncut and cut bands
Mutation that destroys a site reverses it: uncut = mutant
Sickle cell mutation destroys an MstII site
